reference: Procps-ng watch is the independent oracle for parser rejection only. Bounded non-terminal operations use the documented custom watch behavior with fixed frame and private-file expectations. Bash type/help checks are metadata, not operation coverage.
coverage: Bash registration and help metadata (not operation coverage).
Five independent Procps-ng parser rejection comparisons.
Bounded single failed child with -e/-x, two deterministic frames with -g, and two-frame custom -d/-C capture in private relative files.
exclusions: No unbounded monitor, host process signals, host system mutations, or network activity.
Actual terminal frames, cadence, interactive SIGINT, and beep behavior remain unverified.

cases.purpose: Bash type -t reports the statically enabled watch command as a builtin.
The static and packaged builtin expose the complete documented option synopsis.
The help entry contains the documented invocation forms for the interval, exec, failure, change, diff, no-title, precise, and capture options.
cases.script:
doc=$(help watch)
for option in '-n SEC' '-x CMD' '-b CMD' '-e CMD' '-g CMD' '-d CMD' '-t|--no-title' '-p|--precise' '-C FILE CMD'; do
  [[ $doc == *"$option"* ]] || exit 1
done
printf 'documented watch options present\n'

cases.purpose: An unparseable -n value is rejected before the harmless watched command can start; procps watch exits 1 for this parse error.
Omitting the watched command is a usage error and starts no operation; procps watch exits 1 for this usage error.
An unsupported option is rejected during parsing before any watched command starts; procps watch exits 1 for this option error.
Missing -n operand is rejected during option parsing; no watched command can start.
Accepted no-title and precise long options still lead to independent interval parser rejection, with no child execution.
Documented custom -e exits with failure after exactly one harmless failing builtin child; -x selects direct argv execution.
Custom non-terminal -g emits two deterministic small frames and exits on their change; the private counter must be exactly two. This exercises ordinary file writes.
cases.script:
watch -n 0.01 -g 'n=0; if test -f count; then read -r n < count; fi; n=$((n + 1)); printf "%s\n" "$n" > count; printf "%s\n" "$n"'
[[ $(< count) == 2 ]]

cases.purpose: The documented custom -C capture contains two iteration markers and -d reverse-video bytes for the changed digit. Deterministic private counter changes on the second frame; no PTY or procps byte equality is claimed.
cases.script:
watch -n 0.01 -g -d -C frames 'n=0; if test -f count; then read -r n < count; fi; n=$((n + 1)); printf "%s\n" "$n" > count; printf "%s\n" "$n"'
[[ $(< count) == 2 ]]
expected=$'--- iteration 1 ---\n1\n--- iteration 2 ---\n\e[7m2\e[27m\n'
read_status=0
IFS= read -r -d '' actual < frames || read_status=$?
[[ $read_status == 1 ]]
[[ $actual == "$expected" ]]

cases.purpose: Compare real terminal rendering, interactive errors, and terminal interaction with Procps-ng watch.
cases.reason: Remaining obligations: r3: The candidate message, key wait and keyed exit were never reached. Preserve the existing legacy bounded-execution companion.; r6: A width 40 redraw follows resize, coincident with the ordinary one-second update. The data do not distinguish the named SIGWINCH path from periodic polling; retain partial without imposing an unstated exact-latency threshold.

cases.purpose: A bounded relative helper prints one argument and exits nonzero. Direct -x execution must preserve spaces and a semicolon literally, and -e must stop after that first child.
cases.script:
printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/sh' 'printf "<%s>\n" "$1"' 'exit 7' > helper
chmod 700 helper
watch -n 0.01 -e -x ./helper 'arg;two words'
